title: TB7-08407
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated April 18, 2017, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated April 18, 2017, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), I confirm the determination of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal is dismissed.

The Appellant is a citizen of Kyrgyzstan. She also has residency status in Kazakhstan that expires in XXXX 2018. She fears persecution in both countries based on her religious beliefs and on her nationality as an ethnic Russian. The Appellant is an Evangelical Christian. She left Kyrgyzstan for Kazakhstan in XXXX 2006.

The RPD had credibility concerns regarding elements of the story related to her time in Kazakhstan. In relation to Kyrgyzstan, the RPD found that the documentary evidence does not demonstrate that that Evangelical Christians and/or ethnic Russians have a well-founded fear of persecution in Kyrgyzstan today.

The Appellant argues that the RPD mischaracterized the evidence of the human rights situation in both Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan by undertaking a selective analysis of the documentation. She also maintains that RPD findings were speculative and in effect dictated how she should practice her faith. The Appellant believes that the RPD made incorrect findings of fact related to the ability to proselytize in both Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan and that the RPD erred in its credibility findings.

While I agree that the RPD did twice incorrectly characterize the documentary evidence, overall I believe the RPD correctly found that there is no objective basis for the Appellant's fear in Kyrgyzstan.

I accept that the Appellant is an Evangelical Christian and an ethnic Russian. The determinative issue is this appeal is whether there is an objective basis for the Appellant's fear in Kyrgyzstan. Kyrgyzstan is the Appellant's country of citizenship and given that I find she has no fear of persecution there, I need not consider the RPD's credibility and documentary findings in relation to Kazakhstan. New National Documentation Package

On January 16, 2018, I disclosed the 2016 version of the International Religious Freedom Report for 2016: Kyrgyz Republic (the IRFR) to the Appellant. On January 19, I received a response from the Appellant's counsel requesting that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) consider admitting the entire new National Documentation Package (NDP) package for Kyrgyzstan, of which the IRFR is included. Counsel also provided submissions on the documentation contained in the new NDP.1
I agree with the Appellant on this matter and I admit the new NDP into evidence as part of my specialized knowledge.2 ANALYSIS

A key argument of the Appellant is that the RPD selectively viewed the objective documentary evidence, ignoring elements that are not consistent with its decision. In addition, the Appellant maintains that the RPD incorrectly speculated that: "nothing in the recent report indicates that the claimant could not rejoin her church ..."3 and incorrectly stated that "nothing in the documentary evidence indicates that the claimant cannot own or possess a bible."4

Regarding the specific errors referenced by the Appellant, I find that the RPD did err in stating that nothing in the evidence indicates that individuals cannot own or possess bibles. It is true that according to Kyrgyz law, religious materials should only be stored and used in places designated by the law, i.e. in a registered Church, etc. On the face of the law it appears the RPD is incorrect.

I also agree that the RPD erred by speculating that the Appellant's specific Church in XXXX was still likely in place and able to welcome the Appellant. The Appellant offered no evidence in this regard and there was nothing specific on this particular church in the documentation.

Notwithstanding these two errors, I find that the RPD decision itself is correct. I agree with the RPD that the preponderance of evidence suggests that the Appellant could return to Kyrgyzstan and live as an ethnic Russian and worship as an Evangelical Christian. The RPD thoroughly reviewed the evidence on the situation in Kyrgyzstan and found no evidence of an on-going risk to the Appellant either because of her faith or her ethnicity. I also find that, contrary to the arguments of the Appellant, the RPD did look at the practical implementation of religious freedom laws. While I agree with the RPD findings and assessment of the evidence, I will review specific elements of the documentation here in order to respond to certain concerns raised by the Appellant. Registration Difficulties and Evangelical Christian Groups

The Appellant is correct that religious congregations, groups and churches must register with the State Commission on Religious Affairs (SCRA). The SCRA may deny registration to certain religious groups, and unregistered groups cannot legally rent space and hold religious services. Denied applicants may reapply or appeal to the courts. The law provides for the right of religious groups to produce, import, export, and distribute religious literature. The law prohibits the distribution of religious literature and materials in public locations or in visits to individual households, schools, and other institutions.5

In practice, the evidence suggests that non-Russian orthodox Christian congregations and churches have had difficulty registering for some time and certainly since 2009.6 I accept that the registration process is arbitrary and creates tremendous uncertainty and stress on those organisations wishing to register. I can also understand that this situation would contribute to a climate of fear amongst those wishing to register their churches or organisations.

However, I also note that according to the U.S. International Religious Freedoms Report on Kyrgyzstan for 2015, despite these laws, unregistered churches and groups "held regular religious services without Government interference."7 The same source states that violations of the registration law may result in an administrative fine of 500 soms, or approximately US$7. Similarly, the penalty for distributing religious literature outside of the prescribed registered centres is a monetary fine.8

I find that the Appellant, as an Evangelical Christian, could practice at one of the already registered Evangelical churches and groups in Kyrgyzstan. In her Basis of Claim form, the Appellant stated that Evangelical Christian groups include Baptists, Pentecostals and Charismatics.9 The 2016 International Religious Freedoms Report on Kyrgyzstan states that there are 50 Baptist, 56 Pentecostal and 43 Charismatic organisations registered in the country.10 The Appellant could practice her faith with one of these legally registered groups.

Were the Appellant to decide to worship with an unregistered church, it appears from the documentary evidence that these organisations face only administrative fines for lack of registration. I could find no report of attacks or mistreatment of Evangelical Christians in the documentation. In the submissions that accompanied the new evidence in this appeal, Appellant's counsel draws my attention to the following: Religious groups acting inconsistently with the law may be fined or deported. Violations of the law may result in fines in the amount of 1000 soms ($14), and deportation in the case of foreign missionaries.11

Counsel argues that this passage, and the new IRFR report in general, confirms that the Appellant cannot practice her religion. I respectfully disagree. As I noted earlier, there are many registered and legal Evangelical Christian groups registered in Kyrgyzstan. The quotation immediately above states that religious groups that act inconsistently with the law face fines (or deportation for foreign citizens).

The specific references to difficulties faced by Christians in Kyrgyzstan, including in the country documentation provided by the Appellant, relates almost exclusively to Jehovah Witnesses and converts to Christianity. There have been at least two or three instances where family members have had difficulty properly burying their loved ones who had converted from Islam to Christianity. Jehovah Witnesses have difficulty registering in Kyrgyzstan12 and have faced discrimination (two Jehovah Witness women were placed in house arrest for 31 months and charged with witchcraft. They were freed in 2015) and at least one attack in the past.13

However, I find that the Appellant, as an Evangelical Christian Russian woman, is not similarly situated to either Christian converts or Jehovah Witnesses. If she were to worship at an unregistered church, I accept that she may face a fine or even bureaucratic harassment due to the group not being registered. I do not find that these risks amounts to persecution. The Appellant's Ability to Proselytize

In her Basis of Claim form, the Appellant alleges that she left Kyrgyzstan in 2006 due to ethnic tensions and religious persecution that followed a March 2005 revolution.14 She feared that she was no longer able to share her beliefs publically with her neighbours (i.e. proselytize). At the RPD hearing, she recounts an era of general instability without giving any specific information on the types of religious persecution she observed, heard of or experienced, beyond stating that her Church in XXXX had registration problems and difficulties finding a place to worship. She testifies that she fears arrest but doesn't provide examples of similarly situated individuals who have been arrested. She spoke largely in generalities.15 Her description of the situation and her fear of arrest stands in contrast to recent country documentation, including the new evidence accepted as evidence in this appeal, where I find little reference to problems beyond those I've already summarized.

The Appellant testified that proselytizing is illegal and this is an important element of her faith. I agree that according to law proselytizing is illegal in Kyrgyzstan. However, I could find no evidence in the record of individuals being targeted because of their proselytizing activities. It is disturbing that there has been one reported incident of prolonged house arrest for two Jehovah Witnesses and evidence of one attack on a group of Jehovah Witnesses over the past few years. And, as stated earlier, I could find no reference to arrests or harassment of Evangelical Christians for proselytizing or for any other reason. Furthermore, I have no evidence before me that suggests that the enforcement of the law would be anything beyond a fine should it occur, similar to the consequences for illegally distributing religious materials. I also note that the two problems I could find in the documentation related to Jehovah Witnesses appear to have been isolated incidents.

Refugee protection is forward looking and I have to assess the current risk to the Appellant were she to return. Ultimately, I find that there is insufficient objective evidence before me16 to indicate that Evangelical Christians who proselytize would face persecutory, or indeed any, repercussions in Kyrgyzstan today. I find on a balance of probabilities, that if there were recent incidents of persecution of Christians for proselytizing, there would be some documentation of this by reliable sources. Were the Appellant to proselytize upon her return to Kyrgyzstan, I find that she would not face a serious possibility of persecution. Does the Appellant Face Risk due to her Russian Ethnicity?

The Appellant testified to anti-Russian sentiment prevalent after the March 2006 revolution. She speculated that Russia could lose its status in the country, that jobs are difficult to find and that Russians are leaving Kyrgyzstan.17 In her Basis of Claim form and in testimony, she spoke in generalities and speculated about problems facing Russians. I note that she has no recent experience living in Kyrgyzstan. Given this, my assessment of the risk faced by ethnic Russians in Kyrgyzstan must be based primarily on a review of the objective documentation.

I agree with the RPD that the Appellant would not face more than a mere possibility of persecution in Kyrgyzstan on account of her Russian ethnicity. Having reviewed the human rights reports for Kyrgyzstan in the NDP, including in the new September 2017 NDP, I could find no reference to difficulties faced by ethnic Russians. The reports do speak to problems faced by ethnic Uzbeks, so I am not suggesting that minorities do not face difficulties in Kyrgyzstan. However, Russians account for eight percent of the population of Kyrgyzstan and are represented in Parliament. Russian is an official language of Kyrgyzstan.18 I find on a balance of probabilities that if there were recent incidents of persecution of ethnic Russians there would be some documentation of this by reliable sources. Ultimately, I find that there is insufficient objective evidence before me to indicate that ethnic Russians face persecution in Kyrgyzstan.

I have considered whether there is a serious possibility that the Appellant would be persecuted if she, as an ethnic Russian, were to return to Kyrgyzstan and chooses to practice her faith in either a registered or unregistered church. I have been guided by the country condition documents in evidence. Ultimately I find that the Appellant would not face a serious possibility of persecution were she to return to Kyrgyzstan.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection and dismisses the appeal.
